[Source 1 — reason.com] (URL: https://reason.com/2026/10/12/inside-the-trump-administrations-war-on-the-hague/?utm_source=bluesky&utm_medium=social_reason_non_paid&utm_campaign=reason_brand):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Inside the Trump administration's war on the Hague

In the name of national sovereignty, the U.S. government is trying to ban foreign governments—and American citizens—from voluntarily working with a war crimes tribunal.

Actual Article Body:
Log In

Create new account

Human rights

Matthew Petti
			
						|
			10.12.2026 9:45 AM

The Nobel Peace Prize announcement last week was an awkward moment in U.S.-European relations. The Nobel Committee in Norway awarded the prize to Navi Pillay, a South African judge who used to lead the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague. Hours later, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced yet another round of economic sanctions against the court, vowing to "end the ICC." Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, whose country hosts the ICC, told reporters that he would use "every available means to protect the functioning of the court." And several other U.S. allies issued statements supporting the ICC.

Just before the Nobel showdown, a lawsuit by Americans challenging the anti-ICC campaign moved forward. Matthew Smith, a researcher who provided information to the ICC about atrocities in Myanmar, and Akila Radhakrishnan, a lawyer who had been helping the ICC prosecute the Taliban's crimes against women, have sued President Donald Trump over Executive Order 14203, a February 2025 measure banning Americans from providing "services" to the ICC. Smith and Radhakrishnan argue that the order violates their First Amendment right to share facts and analysis. On September 28, a judge ruled that there is a "strong likelihood" that this is correct, allowing the case to proceed.

The campaign against the ICC has many ironies. One is that Rubio himself used to sing the court's praises. As a senator, he cosponsored a 2022 resolution demanding that the ICC prosecute the Russian invasion of Ukraine and applauding the tribunal's mission "to uphold the rule of law, especially in areas where no rule of law exists." A bigger irony is that, in the name of protecting national sovereignty, the administration is trying to restrict both the decisions other nations can make and the ability of Americans to communicate across borders. And Trump has made it clear that these actions are to protect a foreign country.

Executive Order 14203 begins by condemning the ICC's "illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel." (In fact, the ICC has not issued warrants against Americans, only Israelis.) Rubio is "not trying to defend me. He's trying to defend Bibi and various other people," Trump said at a July 2026 cabinet meeting, using a nickname for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The ICC does not have any power beyond what members give it. The court was created by the Rome Statute of 1998, in which 137 countries agreed to cooperate to prosecute genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression. The United States and Russia signed but then later withdrew their signatures. Unless the U.N. Security Council made a unanimous referral—which would require Russian and U.S. consent—the new court in The Hague could try only crimes involving the citizens or territory of Rome Statute parties. The ICC also asserts that it won't try crimes that are already covered by domestic courts.

The ICC is often confused with an older institution in The Hague, the International Court of Justice, created in 1945 to resolve disputes between U.N. members. Unlike the ICC, the International Court of Justice has no ability to prosecute individuals.

Despite leaving the Rome Statute, the U.S. government worried that its officials could be prosecuted for their interventions in foreign countries. In 2002, President George W. Bush signed the American Service-Members' Protection Act, nicknamed the "Hague Invasion Act," which authorizes "all means necessary and appropriate to bring about the release of any U.S. or allied personnel" in ICC custody. After becoming Trump's national security advisor in 2018, the ultra-hawkish former Bush official John Bolton declared the ICC's very existence "an assault on the constitutional rights of the American People and the sovereignty of the United States."

In 2020, the ICC began investigating atrocities in member state Afghanistan, raising the possibility that it could indeed fulfill Bolton's fears of prosecuting Americans. Trump declared a "national emergency" and froze the bank accounts of two ICC officials. (So far, the court has issued warrants only against members of the new Taliban government, and the prosecution says that it "prioritizes" prosecuting crimes by the Taliban and the Islamic State group.) Beginning in 2023, at the urging of member state Ukraine, the court has issued warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, for their actions on Ukrainian soil. President Joe Biden shared intelligence about the Russian invasion to support the ICC prosecution.

Most controversially, the ICC recognized Palestine as a state in 2015. The move followed a 2014 war between Israel and Hamas, a Palestinian group opposed to the official Palestinian Authority. The U.S. government mobilized to protect Israel from any legal action. President Barack Obama tried to pressure Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas out of seeking ICC membership, and Congress passed a law automatically cutting off aid to Palestinians over any move "that subjects Israeli nationals to an investigation for alleged crimes against Palestinians."

Following the October 2023 attacks by Hamas and the subsequent Israeli invasion of Gaza, the ICC issued arrest warrants against leaders on both sides. Of course, Hamas officials didn't plan to travel anywhere that they could be prosecuted, and all three leaders named by the ICC ended up dead anyways. On the other hand, the ICC warrants could potentially block Netanyahu from traveling anywhere in the First World. Letting Netanyahu visit Europe again became a major focus of Israeli diplomacy.

And U.S. diplomacy. "This court is for Africa and thugs like Putin," the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R–S.C.) reportedly said, according to former ICC prosecutor Karim Khan. Biden called the warrant against Netanyahu "outrageous," accusing the court of making a false "equivalence" between Israel and Hamas. But the Biden administration tread carefully about attacking the ICC head on, given its importance to Ukraine. Netanyahu said in a 2024 interview with former Trump administration official Morgan Ortagus that he was "surprised and disappointed" that Biden wouldn't support "bipartisan" sanctions against ICC officials.

The second Trump administration was far more eager. Last month, U.S. Ambassador Matthew Whittaker demanded that all NATO countries pull out of the ICC, warning them that "we will be watching closely who stands with America." And thanks to Executive Order 14203, these threats have teeth. The Trump administration has been overturning individual ICC judges' lives under the order, which bans the ICC from interacting with the U.S. economy. Canadian judge Kimberly Prost, for example, reported that her bank account and credit cards were frozen, along with her accounts with Amazon, Google, and Expedia. In July 2025, the State Department sanctioned three Palestinian charities that had urged the ICC to investigate Israeli air raids.

The administration even used Executive Order 14203 to target the Italian academic Francesca Albanese, who has no official role with the ICC but wrote a report for the UN Human Rights Council recommending prosecutions of people and companies involved in the Israeli war effort. Albanese's husband, who works at the World Bank in Washington, had his apartment seized by the U.S. Treasury. The couple was banned from visiting their American daughter.

In other words, any public figure of consequence anywhere outside America who calls Netanyahu a criminal can be relentlessly persecuted by the U.S. government. That sure sounds like the kind of one-world government that Bolton and Rubio have warned about, using its powers against offenses far lighter than the crimes the ICC investigates. And unlike the ICC, the U.S. Treasury's sanctions enforcement arm gives neither the accused the right to defend themselves in court nor other countries the right to opt out.

The real question is how far the administration will go preventing American citizens from talking to the court. So far, American companies (and even non-American companies) have obeyed U.S. sanctions against ICC judges. This handful of customers, it seems, is not worth being fined or losing access to the U.S. dollar system. But individual Americans may also want to talk to the court because they have information about war crimes in Ukraine or the Congo, and the U.S. government has tried to push the limits of how it defines sanctionable services.

The Trump administration has "raised a Sword of Damocles over the heads of Plaintiffs and others who wish to communicate with the ICC but are chilled from doing so," lawyers for Smith and Radhakrishnan told the court. "Whether Plaintiffs or others like them may speak to the ICC without falling afoul of the Order and Regulations depends on what they say."

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes
            corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms. Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

Experts have long warned that immigration dragnets and the erosion of civil rights for immigrants will inevitably result in the erosion of rights for citizens.

âIâm a U.S. citizen, please help me.â

Since the start of this Trump administration, weâve watched those warnings come true.

The Trump administration says none of this is happening.

âDHS is NOT arresting U.S. citizens by mistake.â âThere are no âindiscriminateâ stops.â Allegations of âracial profiling are disgusting, reckless and categorically FALSE.â âThe pattern is NOT of law enforcement using force.â âICE does not zip tie or restrain children.â

But that is precisely what is happening, and at a far larger scale than previously reported.

We know because we have once again done what the government hasnât:

We have tallied and cataloged every case we can find of an immigration agent holding a citizen during the current administration.

More than 500 cases. That includes:

More than a hundred Americans held after agents questioned their citizenship. Nearly all were people of color.

At least 70 American children and teens detained, some of whom were handcuffed.

Of the more than 300 Americans we tracked as detained for allegedly assaulting or obstructing agents, we found fewer than half were actually charged in federal court, and many of those cases were dropped or dismissed.

At least 63 Americans detained while recording.

36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or their family.

Roughly a dozen citizens deported, mostly children.

Collectively, these cases show that as the administration has relentlessly pursued immigrants, federal agents have run roughshod over the constitutional rights of citizens too.

Weâre showing you every case â the reality that the administration denies â along with the receipts.

In January 2025, agents held a 21-year-old citizen at gunpoint and put him in handcuffs during a raid at the Philadelphia car wash where he worked.

In April, a 20-year-old was held in a Florida jail for more than 24 hours, despite having proof of his citizenship.

In June, a dual citizen of Mexico and the U.S. was detained while working in California. He was held for four days without access to a lawyer or his family.

During the enforcement surge in Chicago last fall, known as Operation Midway Blitz, there were âno administrative arrests of U.S. citizens,â according to the Department of Homeland Security. âICE has significant protections in place to ensure U.S. citizens are not arrested, detained, or mistakenly removed.â But we found that federal agents detained more than 120 citizens in Illinois during the height of the surge.

In November, agents took an 18-year-old citizen off the street, eventually dumping him in the woods.

In December, an American in Baltimore was picked up and held for 25 days, unable to see her 5-year-old son over Christmas.

In April, when agents stopped a man in Texas, he told them, âIâm a citizen, itâs fine.â He was deported four days later.

In May, a New York teen was thrown to the ground, bloodied and then dumped in an unfamiliar neighborhood. âHe just grabbed me and threw me on the floor,â the teen recalled.

Actual Article Body:
Dan is a managing editor at Raw Story based in Colorado, producing and editing breaking political news.

Dan previously worked as a news associate at The Associated Press in Philadelphia, and later as local editor, breaking news editor and eventually manager at Patch, overseeing the company’s breaking news and Long Island/Hudson Valley teams.

Dan has covered major breaking stories such as mass shootings and wildfires in California, and overseen teams that covered George Santos and the Gilgo Beach serial killings.

A native of Colorado and the Philadelphia area, Dan graduated with a degree in journalism from Temple University.

A clinical and forensic psychologist breaking down President Donald Trump’s weekend rally in Tennessee flagged a moment he called “a really wild thing to watch”: Trump told the crowd he could say the stupidest things and they’d clap, and they did.

Dr. John Paul Garrison, known online as “Dr. G” to more than half a million YouTube subscribers, broke down the Clarksville event in a new video. Trump appeared Saturday at the F&M Bank Arena to campaign for Tennessee Republicans, including Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the GOP nominee for governor, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

“When you stand up here, it’s just like the love. I could say the stupidest things and you clap,” Trump told the audience, which cheered. “You know, I love you so. That’s true.”

Garrison called it “clapping after a thinly veiled insult, basically saying that they would clap for anything.”

“You notice how at the end he said it’s true because he’s emphasizing the fact there is unconditional loyalty no matter what he says,” Garrison said. “Not surprisingly, he goes on to say that he doesn’t say stupid things, but what this does is this is using authority and dominance, and framing it as humor.”

Garrison also zeroed in on a recurring sideways shift of Trump’s jaw that appeared when the president grew animated, including as he boasted about renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America.”

“Sometimes we see that when people are either on stimulant medication or taking stimulants of some kind,” Garrison said, adding that the movement could also have a neurological cause tied to impaired motor functioning. Garrison has not examined Trump, and the White House has not disclosed that the president takes any stimulant medication.

On nights like Saturday, Garrison said, Trump appeared “more emotionally dysregulated” and “almost manic,” struggling to inhibit his own behavior.

Garrison stressed at the start of his video that his analysis “is not a psychological evaluation of any kind” and reflects his opinions. He isn’t the first mental health professional to raise alarms about Trump’s public behavior, and a former GOP strategist said one Trump rally showed he was fading.

Trump, 80, said after a May exam at Walter Reed that “Everything checked out PERFECTLY,” and his White House physician declared him “fully fit” to serve. In a February Reuters/Ipsos poll, 61% of Americans, including 30% of Republicans, said Trump has “become erratic with age.”

Dan is a managing editor at Raw Story based in Colorado, producing and editing breaking political news.

Dan previously worked as a news associate at The Associated Press in Philadelphia, and later as local editor, breaking news editor and eventually manager at Patch, overseeing the company’s breaking news and Long Island/Hudson Valley teams.

Dan has covered major breaking stories such as mass shootings and wildfires in California, and overseen teams that covered George Santos and the Gilgo Beach serial killings.

A native of Colorado and the Philadelphia area, Dan graduated with a degree in journalism from Temple University.

A clinical and forensic psychologist breaking down President Donald Trump’s weekend rally in Tennessee flagged a moment he called “a really wild thing to watch”: Trump told the crowd he could say the stupidest things and they’d clap, and they did.

Dr. John Paul Garrison, known online as “Dr. G” to more than half a million YouTube subscribers, broke down the Clarksville event in a new video. Trump appeared Saturday at the F&M Bank Arena to campaign for Tennessee Republicans, including Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the GOP nominee for governor, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

“When you stand up here, it’s just like the love. I could say the stupidest things and you clap,” Trump told the audience, which cheered. “You know, I love you so. That’s true.”

Garrison called it “clapping after a thinly veiled insult, basically saying that they would clap for anything.”

“You notice how at the end he said it’s true because he’s emphasizing the fact there is unconditional loyalty no matter what he says,” Garrison said. “Not surprisingly, he goes on to say that he doesn’t say stupid things, but what this does is this is using authority and dominance, and framing it as humor.”

Garrison also zeroed in on a recurring sideways shift of Trump’s jaw that appeared when the president grew animated, including as he boasted about renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America.”

“Sometimes we see that when people are either on stimulant medication or taking stimulants of some kind,” Garrison said, adding that the movement could also have a neurological cause tied to impaired motor functioning. Garrison has not examined Trump, and the White House has not disclosed that the president takes any stimulant medication.

On nights like Saturday, Garrison said, Trump appeared “more emotionally dysregulated” and “almost manic,” struggling to inhibit his own behavior.

Garrison stressed at the start of his video that his analysis “is not a psychological evaluation of any kind” and reflects his opinions. He isn’t the first mental health professional to raise alarms about Trump’s public behavior, and a former GOP strategist said one Trump rally showed he was fading.

Trump, 80, said after a May exam at Walter Reed that “Everything checked out PERFECTLY,” and his White House physician declared him “fully fit” to serve. In a February Reuters/Ipsos poll, 61% of Americans, including 30% of Republicans, said Trump has “become erratic with age.”
